'''Russell James Donnelly''' (born 16 April 1930 in [[Hamilton, Ontario]], died 13 June 2015 in [[Eugene, Oregon]]) was a [[Canadian-American]] physicist known for his work on classical and quantum fluid dynamics.<ref name=phystoday>{{cite journal|last1=Hammer|first1=Philip W.|last2=Sreenivasan|first2=Katepalli R.|last3=Niemela|first3=Joseph J.|title=Russell James Donnelly|journal=Physics Today|date=1 October 2015|volume=68|issue=10|pages=59–60|doi=10.1063/PT.3.2954|bibcode = 2015PhT....68j..59H |doi-access=}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://pages.uoregon.edu/rjd/curriculum.htm|title=Russell J. Donnelly|work=uoregon.edu|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131123110458/http://pages.uoregon.edu/rjd/curriculum.htm|archivedate=2013-11-23}}</ref><ref name="Spotlight">{{cite journal |title=Member in the Spotlight: Russell Donnelly |website=www.aps.org |url=https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/199512/donnelly.cfm |date=1995 |language=en}}</ref> He connected the fields of [[low temperature physics]] and [[fluid turbulence]].<ref name="Niemela"/>

==Life==
Donnelly graduated from [[McMaster University]] with a bachelor's degree in 1951 and a master's degree in 1952.<ref name=phystoday /> In 1956 he received his doctorate from [[Yale University]], with a thesis entitled "On the hydrodynamics of liquid helium". His doctoral advisers were the noted physicists [[C. T. Lane]] and [[Lars Onsager]].<ref name="Niemela"/> His PhD work demonstrated that the oscillations of liquid helium in a U-tube at a low temperature could be described by two-phase liquid theory.<ref name=phystoday />

In 1956 he became an instructor and later professor at the [[James Franck Institute]] at the [[University of Chicago]], where he worked with [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar|S. Chandrasekhar]] and Dave Fultz. From 1959 - 1963 he was Sloan Fellow.  In 1966 he moved to the [[University of Oregon]],<ref name=phystoday /> where it was possible for both himself and his wife, art historian Marian Donnelly, to hold positions.<ref name="Niemela"/>  He eventually served twice as department chair at the University of Oregon.<ref name=phystoday /> In 1972 he worked at the Niels Bohr Institute in Copenhagen. He was also a visiting professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara and the University of Birmingham. He was a consultant at NASA and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory.<ref name="Niemela">{{cite journal |last1=Niemela |first1=J.j. |last2=Sreenivasan |first2=K.r. |title=Russell Donnelly and His Leaks |journal=Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics |date=10 March 2022 |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=33–47 |doi=10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-050521-033802 |bibcode=2022ARCMP..13...33N |issn=1947-5454|doi-access=free }}</ref>

During his life he advised 25 PhD students, and mentored many others, including future Nobel prize winner [[David Lee (physicist)|David Lee]].<ref name=phystoday /> He died from pneumonia on 13 June 2015 in Eugene, Oregon.<ref name=phystoday /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://around.uoregon.edu/content/physicist-russ-donnelly-pioneer-science-cold-dies-85|title=Physicist Russ Donnelly, a pioneer in the science of cold, dies at 85 |date=June 16, 2015 |work=Around the O |publisher=University of Oregon}}</ref>

* 2002, [[Fritz London Memorial Prize]], [[International Union of Pure and Applied Physics]]<ref name="London">{{cite web |title=Fritz London Memorial Prize |url=https://physics.duke.edu/fritz-london-memorial-prize |website=Duke University |access-date=21 March 2022}}</ref>
* 2001, Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]<ref name="AAAS">{{cite web |title=Russell J. Donnelly |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/russell-j-donnelly |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |access-date=21 March 2022 |language=en}}</ref>
*2001, Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]<ref name="AAAS2001">{{cite journal |title=American Academy Elects New Members |journal=Physics Today |date=August 2001 |volume=54 |issue=8 |pages=60–61 |doi=10.1063/1.2405665 |bibcode=2001PhT....54T..60. |url=https://physicstoday.scitation.org/doi/pdf/10.1063/1.2405665 |access-date=21 March 2022 |language=en |issn=0031-9228|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* 1999, Honorary doctorate, McMaster University<ref name="Honorary">{{cite web |title=McMaster University Honorary Degree Recipients (Chronological) 1892-Present |url=https://secretariat.mcmaster.ca/app/uploads/Honorary_Degrees_Recipients_1982-2021.pdf |website=McMaster University |access-date=21 March 2022}}</ref>
* 1996, Lars [[Onsager Medal]], [[Norwegian University of Science and Technology]]<ref name="NTNU">{{cite web |title=The Lars Onsager Lecture - NTNU |url=https://www.ntnu.edu/onsager/lecture |website=Norwegian University of Science and Technology |access-date=21 March 2022}}</ref>
* 1975, [[Otto Laporte Award]], Division of Fluid Dynamics, [[American Physical Society]]<ref name="DFD">{{cite web |title=Prizes & Awards |url=https://engage.aps.org/dfd/honors/prizes-awards/otto-laporte-award |website=Division of Fluid Dynamics |publisher=American Physical Society |access-date=21 March 2022}}</ref>
*1963, Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (APS)<ref name="APSF">{{cite web |title=APS Fellow Archive |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=D&year=&unit_id=&institution= |website=American Physical Society |access-date=21 March 2022 |language=en}}</ref>
* Fellow of the Institute of Physics
